explain.tweet: What a thing is ≠ that it is. A lion's nature doesn't include its existing, so it can't give itself being—it must receive it, right now. A chain of receivers explains nothing; it must end in what IS existence itself: one, necessary, uncaused. That's God. #Aquinas
explain.elevator: Everything around us has a *what* and a *that*. You can know exactly what a lion is without knowing whether lions exist — so existence isn't part of a lion's nature. It must get existence from something else, not just once but at every moment. If that source merely has existence too, it needs a source as well. The chain must end in something whose very nature is to exist — and there can be only one such thing. That's what we call God.
explain.twoMinute:
Here's the core idea. Think of anything — a dog, a tree, you. There are two different things you can know about it. One is *what* it is: its nature, its essence. The other is *that* it is: the fact that it actually exists. These really are different. I can describe a lion, a pterodactyl, and a unicorn in full detail, and you still couldn't tell me which one is alive today, which is extinct, and which never existed. Knowing what something is doesn't tell you whether it is.

So for ordinary things, existence isn't part of the package of what they are. That means they don't exist on their own steam. And they can't give themselves existence either — you'd have to already exist to do anything, including giving yourself existence. So whatever has existence without *being* existence has to be receiving it from something else.

And not just in the past. Your parents explain how you got started, but right now, this second, your existence still isn't built into your nature. So something must be keeping you in being right now.

Now suppose that something is also the kind of thing that merely *has* existence. Then it needs a source too, right now, and so on. That's a chain of borrowers passing along something none of them owns — like an infinite stack of IOUs with no money behind it. The chain has to end in something that doesn't borrow existence at all, something whose very essence *is* to exist. Aquinas calls it subsistent existence itself.

And there can only be one of those. To have two, you'd need something to tell them apart — but anything added to ‘existence itself’ makes it ‘existence itself plus something,’ which is no longer existence itself. So it's unique, which means everything else depends on it. It can't fail to exist, it has no cause, and it has no unrealized potential. Which means it's changeless, timeless, immaterial, all-powerful, and — as the book argues — intelligent and good. That's not a being among beings. That's what classical theism has always meant by God.

Notice what I didn't say: I never said the universe had a beginning, and I never said ‘everything has a cause.’ Only what *has* existence needs a cause. What *is* existence doesn't — and couldn't.
explain.eli12:
Imagine you have a drawing of a dragon. You know exactly what it looks like — wings, scales, fire. But knowing what a dragon *is* doesn't make one real. Being *real* is something extra.

That's true of everything: dogs, trees, even you. What you are is one thing; being real is another. So where does your ‘being real’ come from? Not from yourself — you'd have to already be real to give yourself anything.

So something else has to keep you real, right now, like a lamp keeps a room lit. If that something also just *borrows* its realness, it needs a source too. But you can't have an endless line of borrowers and nobody who actually has the thing. There has to be something that doesn't borrow realness at all — something whose whole nature is *being real*.

And there can only be one of those, because anything you added to tell two of them apart would make them ‘being real plus something.’ That one source of everyone's existence is what people mean by God.
whiteboard: Write two columns: WHAT (essence) and THAT (existence). Under WHAT write ‘lion: big cat’, ‘pterodactyl: flying reptile’, ‘unicorn: horned horse’. Under THAT write ‘?’. Say: the first column never fills in the second.

Draw a circle with its radius and circumference. Say: really distinct, never apart — and both follow from what a circle is. Now write ‘lion → exists?’ with a crossed-out arrow: existence does NOT follow from a lion's essence.

Draw a stick-figure dog labeled ‘Fido (now)’. Write ‘existence must be imparted NOW’ and an arrow from outside. Cross out a self-pointing arrow: ‘can't give itself existence — would have to exist first.’
Stack boxes above Fido: C, B, A, each with a ‘receives existence’ arrow from above. Label the stack ‘hierarchical: each gives only while receiving.’ Draw IOU notes beside it.
At the top draw a distinct shape labeled ‘ESSENCE = EXISTENCE (subsistent existence itself)’, with arrows only going down. Say: it gives without receiving.
Next to it, draw two copies labeled A and B with a ‘+F’ and ‘+G’. Cross them out: any difference makes it ‘existence + something’. Write ‘ONLY ONE’.
Write the chain: unique → cause of everything else → necessary → uncaused.
Write ‘essence : existence :: potency : act’ and draw an arrow to ‘PURE ACT (ch. 1)’, then list the attributes: immutable, eternal, immaterial, perfect, omnipotent, good, intelligent, omniscient.
Finish with two crossed-out slogans: ‘The universe had a beginning’ and ‘Everything has a cause.’ Replace with: ‘Whatever HAS existence needs a cause; what IS existence doesn't.’
explain.keyAnalogy: The IOU analogy (Feser's own). A thing whose essence is distinct from its existence is like an IOU: it ‘has’ value only because something else backs it. An existence-imparting cause that itself merely has existence is just another IOU pointing to another. However long the chain — even infinite — it produces no real money unless it is backed by actual cash, something that has value not on loan but in itself. Subsistent existence itself is the ‘cash’: it doesn't have existence on credit; it is existence. Use it after the listener has accepted that a dog can't supply its own existence, and then ask: ‘How many IOUs do you need before you get a dollar?’ Close by noting the analogy's limit: the backing isn't just the first in a line of IOUs but something of a completely different kind.

persuade.coreInsight:
The click comes when a listener sees that **having existence** and **being existence** are different, and that anything which merely *has* existence is, right now, *receiving* it. Once that is grasped, the rest is almost automatic: receivers can't be the ultimate source; a chain of receivers explains nothing; the source must be what *is* existence; and there can be only one such thing.

It usually fails to click for two reasons. First, people hear ‘first cause’ and picture the *earliest* domino, so they think of the Big Bang and an eternal universe, and the argument seems to rest on disputed cosmology. Second, they take existence for granted as the default state of things — ‘stuff just exists, and it takes something to *destroy* it.’ The lion/unicorn contrast and the question ‘what makes a dog real right now, given that ‘dog’ doesn't include ‘real’?’ are the tools for dislodging that assumption.

audiences.startingPoint: Assumes physical stuff simply exists, that persistence is the default (conservation laws), and that ‘first cause’ means the Big Bang.
audiences.approach: Separate the argument cleanly from cosmology at the outset: it works even for an eternal multiverse. Then make the point about physics' own method: laws describe what existing systems do; they presuppose the systems. Use the lion/pterodactyl/unicorn test with a scientific twist — a complete physical description of a particle type doesn't tell you whether any exist; you must look. Present the real distinction as a claim about the logic of scientific knowledge (natures a priori, existence a posteriori). Only then bring in the conservation question and the hierarchical series.
audiences.openingQuestion: If you had the complete physics of a particle that was predicted but not yet detected, could the equations alone tell you whether it exists?
audiences.avoid: Don't lean on the Big Bang, and don't treat ‘God’ as an explanation competing with physics for the same job.

audiences.startingPoint: Believes existence is just instantiation (the existential quantifier) and that ‘existence is not a predicate’ settles the matter.
audiences.approach: Engage Kenny's objection directly and respectfully. Grant that the quantifier captures something. Then press the grounding question: what makes it true that something falls under the concept *cat*? Use Knasas's existence-neutral grasp to defuse the ‘Martians’ argument, and Klima's point that real distinction need not mean separability. Frame the Thomistic act of existence as a proposal about what the quantifier is tracking.
audiences.openingQuestion: When ‘there is an x such that x is a cat’ is true, is it true because of the concept, or because of something about the world?
audiences.avoid: Don't dismiss Frege or treat Kenny as a straw man; don't say ‘existence is a property’ — the Thomist denies that too.

audiences.who: Churchgoing believer who has never heard the argument
audiences.startingPoint: Believes God created the world, but pictures creation as a past event and God as a very great being among beings.
audiences.approach: Show that on this argument creation is ongoing: God is not the one who lit the fuse long ago but the one who keeps everything in being now. Introduce ‘subsistent existence itself’ as a way of understanding why God is not one more thing in the universe. Connect with ‘in him we live and move and have our being’-type intuitions without leaning on Scripture as a premise.
audiences.openingQuestion: If God stopped thinking about you for one second, what do you suppose would happen to you?
audiences.avoid: Don't let the believer treat the argument as a mere restatement of faith; insist that each step stands on reason.

audiences.startingPoint: Expects ‘Everything has a cause, so God’ and has ‘What caused God?’ ready.
audiences.approach: Pre-empt the caricature immediately: the premise is that only things whose essence is distinct from their existence need a cause. Walk through why a dog is such a thing and why a being whose essence is existence couldn't have a cause. Then let them see that ‘What caused God?’ is like asking what makes a triangle's three sides three-sided — it misunderstands what is being claimed.
audiences.openingQuestion: Would you agree that knowing what a unicorn is doesn't tell you whether there are any?
audiences.avoid: Don't get defensive or rhetorical; don't concede ‘everything has a cause’ as the premise, even for simplicity.

audiences.startingPoint: Open-minded, suspects metaphysics is word games, but willing to follow an argument.
audiences.approach: Use the whiteboard sequence. Emphasize that each step is independently checkable and that three separate arguments converge on the real distinction. Invite them to find the weakest step, then address it honestly. Show the payoff: the same conclusion as the Aristotelian and Neoplatonic proofs from a different starting point.
audiences.openingQuestion: What's the difference between knowing what something is and knowing that it is?
audiences.avoid: Don't rush to the attributes or to ‘God’; let them feel the force of the uniqueness argument first.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: So this is another ‘first cause’ argument? Everything has a cause, so there's a first cause, so God?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: No — and that's the most common misreading. The argument never says everything has a cause. It says that anything whose existence isn't part of what it is needs a cause for its existence.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: ‘Existence isn't part of what it is’ — what does that even mean?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Try this. I describe three animals to you in complete detail: a lion, a pterodactyl, a unicorn. One is alive, one is extinct, one never existed. Can you tell which from the descriptions?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Obviously not. I'd have to check the world.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Right. So knowing what a thing is doesn't give you that it is. If a lion's existence were just part of its nature, knowing its nature would tell you it exists. It doesn't.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Maybe I just don't know the lion's nature completely. Existence could be in the part I'm missing.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Here's the test. If you thought a lion wasn't a cat, you'd have a wrong idea of what a lion is. If you thought lions were extinct, you'd be wrong about the world — but your idea of a lion would be fine. So existence isn't one of the features that make up what a lion is.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Okay, suppose essence and existence are different. So what?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Then a lion doesn't exist by its own nature. And it can't give itself existence — to do anything you already have to exist. So its existence has to come from something else.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Sure: its parents. Evolution. No God required.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Parents explain how a lion got started. But right now, this second, the lion's existence still isn't part of its nature. What's supplying it now? Not the parents — they may be dead. Not the lion itself.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Why does it need supplying? Things just keep existing unless something destroys them.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: That's assuming existence is the default for a lion — that it belongs to lions by nature. But we just saw it doesn't. Physics tells you how existing things behave; it doesn't tell you why there's anything there to behave.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Fine, say something is keeping it in existence. Why not an infinite regress of such things?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Because each link would only be passing on existence it's itself receiving at that very moment. It's like an infinite stack of IOUs — you never get a dollar unless something is backed by actual cash. The chain has to end in something that doesn't receive existence at all.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: And what would that be?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Something whose very nature is to exist — not something that has existence, but existence itself. Aquinas calls it subsistent existence itself.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Why not several of those? A committee of necessary beings?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: What would make two of them two? Some extra feature, or some bit of matter. But then each would be ‘existence itself plus something’ — and so not existence itself. There can only be one.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Then what caused *it*?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Nothing could. The need for a cause came from having an essence that isn't existence. This has no such gap. It's not an exception to the rule; the rule doesn't apply.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Even granting all that, why call it God? Maybe it's the universe, or the laws of physics.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: The universe has a definite nature, parts, and could have been otherwise — so it's something that has existence, not existence itself. And existence itself has no unrealized potential, which means it's changeless, timeless, immaterial, and unlimited in power. That's exactly the classical idea of God — and the same being the argument from change reaches.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: I'm not convinced yet, but I admit it's not the argument I thought it was.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: That's a fair start. If you want to attack it, the place to push is the real distinction — and there are three separate arguments for it. Pick the one you think is weakest and we'll look at it.

socratic: Can you tell me what a unicorn is? Does knowing that tell you whether there are any?
If you thought lions were extinct, would you have misunderstood what a lion is, or just be wrong about the world?
Could something that exists by its very nature ever go out of existence?
What would a thing have to do in order to give itself existence? Could it do that without already existing?
Your parents explain how you began. What explains your existing at this very second?
If each link in a chain only passes along what it receives, what would the chain pass along if nothing at the top had it to begin with?
What makes two things of the same kind two rather than one?
If we tried to have two things that were each ‘existence itself’, what would distinguish them — and would they still be existence itself?
Why might something whose nature is existence not need a cause, even if everything else does?
If something has no potential waiting to be realized, could it change? Could it be made of parts or of matter?
Is ‘a circle's radius’ the same thing as ‘its circumference’? Can you have one without the other? What does that tell you about whether ‘distinct’ means ‘separable’?

traps.trap: Presenting the argument as ‘everything has a cause, so God,’ which invites ‘What caused God?’
traps.fix: State the premise precisely from the start: whatever has an essence really distinct from its existence needs a cause of its existence.

traps.trap: Framing it as an argument about the beginning of the universe or the Big Bang.
traps.fix: Say explicitly that it concerns what keeps things in being now and would work even if the universe were eternal.

traps.trap: Describing the real distinction as if essence and existence were separable things, so the listener pictures ‘essences waiting in a warehouse.’
traps.fix: Use the radius/circumference example: really distinct, never apart. Essences don't exist on their own.

traps.trap: Skipping the uniqueness argument, so the listener imagines many necessary beings or a physical necessary being.
traps.fix: Walk through ‘existence itself plus F’ carefully; it is what rules out rivals and makes subsistent existence the cause of everything else.

traps.trap: Leaping from ‘first cause’ to the God of a particular religion without the attribute derivation.
traps.fix: Show the bridge: essence is to existence as potency to act, so subsistent existence is pure act, and pure act has the classical attributes (chapter 1, developed in chapter 6).

traps.trap: Answering Kenny-style or Fregean objections by insisting that existence is a property.
traps.fix: The Thomist denies existence is a property or accident; it is the act by which a thing is real at all. Press the grounding question instead.

traps.trap: Getting lost in jargon (esse, ipsum esse subsistens, per se series) before the listener has the basic intuition.
traps.fix: Start with the lion/unicorn test and Fido right now; introduce the technical terms only as labels for what the listener already sees.

connections.note: The introduction's framework — demonstrations from evident starting points, not probabilistic hypotheses or God-of-the-gaps reasoning — applies here: the starting point (things have an essence and exist) is as evident as anything could be.

The Thomistic proof reuses chapter 1's machinery at every crucial joint: the hierarchical (per se) series and why it can't regress infinitely; the instrumental character of its intermediate members; the replies to Hume, quantum mechanics, and ‘What caused God?’. Above all, essence relates to existence as potency to act, so subsistent existence itself is pure actuality — the very same unique being as the Aristotelian proof's purely actual actualizer, with all the attributes derived there.

Chapter 2 already listed essence and existence among the ‘metaphysical parts’ whose combination needs a cause, and argued that the first cause must be absolutely simple. Chapter 4 takes that particular composition and develops it in depth. Its uniqueness argument (any differentiator makes it ‘existence itself plus F’) closely parallels chapter 2's argument that there can be only one absolutely simple One, and subsistent existence itself — with no distinction of essence and existence — is that simple One.

Chapter 3 argues from abstract objects (universals, propositions, possibilities) to a divine intellect. The Thomistic proof's appeal to real essences and to proportionate causality (for intellect and omniscience) complements it: the essences of things, understood in the divine intellect, are what God gives existence to.

The rationalist proof reaches a necessary being via the principle of sufficient reason. The Thomistic proof supplies a metaphysical account of what necessity is — a being whose essence is its existence — and of why contingent things are contingent: their essence is distinct from their existence.

Stage 2 compresses the derivation of the divine attributes; chapter 6 develops them at length, and the idea of God as subsistent existence itself undergirds divine simplicity, unity, and immutability there.
Chapter 6's treatment of God's knowledge, will, goodness, and relation to creation (conservation and concurrence) builds on the claim here that God imparts existence to all things at every moment.

Chapter 7 answers general objections to natural theology — including charges about the principle of causality, ‘What caused God?’, and the move from first cause to God — that are briefly flagged in this chapter's ‘objections rebutted’ section.

Later objections in chapter 7 lean on this chapter's picture of God. Against scientism: no physical description tells us what imparts existence to physical things. Against the ‘one god further’ jibe: subsistent existence itself is not one more being alongside Zeus and Thor, but the unique source of all beings. And the replies on evil and divine hiddenness presuppose the purely actual, fully good cause established here.

In a capstone synthesis, the Thomistic proof is the deepest of the five convergent routes: change (ch1), composition (ch2), and contingency (ch5) are all, at bottom, cases of things that have existence without being existence.
